title: Predictors of Risk of Cow Mastitis and Management Practices Among Smallholder Dairy Herds, Plateau State, Nigeria
content: Mastitis is a leading cause of reduced milk yield, poor animal welfare, and economic losses in smallholder dairy systems. Data on its prevalence and risk factorsis scarce in Nigeria. We assessed the prevalence of mastitis and management practices among dairy herds in Plateau State, Nigeria. A cross-sectional survey of 300 smallholder dairy farms was conducted, based on farmer-reported clinical mastitis. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and on-farm observations. Herd demographics and management practices were described and Pearson’s chi-square tests evaluated associations between farmer, herd, and management-level factors with mastitis occurrence. The overall prevalence of mastitis was 59.4% (95% CI: 53.7–64.9). Mastitis was strongly associated with farms exhibiting a combination of management deficits: poor milking hygiene (e.g., lack of teat cleaning, χ² = 18.40, p < 0.001), suboptimal herd management (e.g., no separate calving area, χ² = 8.32, p = 0.004), and reliance on non-veterinary diagnosis and treatment (χ² = 7.91, p=0.048; χ² = 26.63, p < 0.001). High antibiotic use without oversight was common. Findings underscore the urgent need for farmer education, veterinary extension services, and policy interventions promoting hygienic milking, evidence-based treatment, and rational antimicrobial use. Adoption of preventive measures such as routine udder checks, dry cow therapy, and proper housing could substantially reduce mastitis burden in Nigerian dairy herds.
